title: Booting, GRUB, systemd & shutdown
about: What happens between power-on and the login prompt: firmware, partition tables, boot loader, kernel, the first process, systemd units and targets, managing services with systemctl, and shutting down cleanly.

questions.title: The boot sequence
questions.text: Put the stages of booting a typical Linux PC in order.

items.t: The firmware (BIOS or UEFI) tests and initialises the hardware
items.why: Nothing can be loaded before the hardware is usable.

items.t: The firmware finds the boot disk and reads its partition table and boot code
items.why: It must know where the boot loader lives.

items.t: The boot loader (for example GRUB) runs and lets you choose a kernel or system
items.why: Stage 1 loads stage 2, which shows the menu.

items.t: The kernel is loaded into memory and starts (with an initial RAM disk)
items.why: The loader hands control over to it.

items.t: The kernel starts the first process (PID 1, normally systemd)
Services start and a login prompt appears
items.why: The system is ready for users.

questions.title: What firmware does
questions.text: What is the job of the firmware (BIOS or UEFI) at power-on?

options.t: To initialise and check the basic hardware, and then find and start a boot loader from a storage device.
options.why: It lives in non-volatile memory on the motherboard.

options.t: To load the kernel modules of the operating system and to set up the drivers for each of the devices.
To start the login shell of the user who owns the machine, once the hardware is ready.
To schedule the processes that run on the machine, from the moment that it is powered on.

questions.title: Why a boot loader
questions.text: Why is a boot loader such as GRUB needed between the firmware and the kernel?

options.t: The firmware loads only a small piece of code; the loader understands file systems, offers a menu, loads the kernel.
Because the kernel cannot run at all unless a graphical menu has been shown to the user by the boot loader first.
Because the firmware cannot read any disk, so another program has to read the disks for it.
options.why: It can read the first blocks or the EFI partition.

options.t: Because GRUB replaces the kernel once the system has started, and runs the machine itself.

questions.title: BIOS and UEFI ideas
questions.text: Match each term with its description.

pairs.r: The older firmware that boots from the first sector (MBR) of a disk
The modern firmware interface, able to start boot loaders from a special FAT partition
A UEFI feature that only starts boot software signed with trusted keys
The old partition table and boot sector layout
The newer partition table that supports many partitions and very large disks

extras.why: None of the terms above is that; GRUB, for one, is a boot loader.

questions.title: MBR limits
questions.text: Which limitation belongs to the classic MBR partitioning scheme?

options.t: At most four primary partitions (or three plus an extended one), and disks above about 2 TB cannot be used.
It cannot hold a Linux file system, so a different scheme is needed for the Linux installations on a machine.
It supports only UEFI firmware, so it cannot be used on machines that boot with a BIOS.
It is limited to a single partition per disk, so the disk cannot be divided in any way.

questions.title: GPT advantages
questions.text: Which is an advantage of GPT over MBR?

options.t: It supports many more partitions (128 by default) and larger disks, keeps a backup of the table, and uses unique IDs.
It is required for every disk that is smaller than 1 GB, which the old scheme cannot handle at all in practice.
It makes the boot slower on purpose, because the table is verified at every start.
It supports only 32-bit systems, which is why it is used on small embedded machines.
options.why: It is used for 64-bit systems as well.

questions.title: The EFI system partition
questions.text: Where does a UEFI system normally keep its boot loaders?

options.t: On a small FAT-formatted partition, the EFI System Partition (ESP), often mounted at `/boot/efi`.
In the first 446 bytes of the disk only, which is where the old BIOS boot code also used to live.
options.why: That is the BIOS/MBR boot code area.

options.t: In `/etc/grub.d`, where the scripts of the loader are stored, next to its menu.
options.why: Configuration fragments, not the boot loader.

options.t: In RAM only, because the firmware loads them from the network at every start.

questions.title: Legacy mode
questions.text: What does "legacy mode" (CSM) mean on a UEFI machine?

options.t: The firmware behaves like a BIOS and boots from the MBR, so that old systems can still start.
options.why: The installation mode must match the partitioning scheme.

options.t: The firmware is disabled, and the machine boots directly from the first disk that it finds, without any checks.
The kernel is loaded twice, once by the firmware and once by the boot loader.
The disk is formatted with an older file system before the boot loader is installed.

questions.title: GRUB files
questions.text: Match each file or directory with its role.

pairs.r: The configuration that GRUB reads at boot
pairs.why: Normally generated, not edited by hand.

pairs.r: General settings such as the default entry and time-out
Scripts that produce parts of the menu

extras.why: That is `grub.cfg`; `/etc/fstab` lists file systems to mount.

questions.title: Editing grub.cfg
questions.text: On Ubuntu and Debian, why should you not edit `/boot/grub/grub.cfg` directly?

options.t: It is generated by `update-grub` from `/etc/default/grub` and `/etc/grub.d/`, so manual edits get overwritten.
Because it is a binary file that can only be changed with the tools of the loader.
Because only the kernel itself is allowed to write to the `/boot` directory of the disk, and not even root can.
Because it is stored in read-only hardware, which cannot be modified by any user.

questions.title: Regenerate the menu
questions.text: After changing `/etc/default/grub`, rebuild the boot menu with: `{{0}}`

wrong.why: That writes the boot loader to a disk; it does not regenerate the menu.
That builds the initial RAM disk.

questions.title: What GRUB can do
questions.text: Which of these can GRUB do?

options.t: Show a menu of systems and kernels, edit boot options, offer a command line, and chain-load other loaders.
Start the user services after the boot, and keep them running until the shutdown.
options.why: That is the job of PID 1.

options.t: Manage the user accounts of the machine, and create new ones for the people who use it when the system starts.
Replace the file system driver of the kernel with one of its own, at each boot.

questions.title: Rescue with GRUB
questions.text: The system does not boot because of a broken menu entry. What does GRUB's command line let you do?

options.t: Set the root device, load a kernel and an initial RAM disk by hand, and boot, to start the machine and repair it.
Edit the passwords of the users directly, so that nobody is locked out of the system when the machine starts.
Update the firmware of the machine, which is the usual cause of a broken menu entry.
Nothing, because GRUB has no interactive mode, and a broken entry means a reinstall.

questions.title: Manual boot from the GRUB prompt
questions.text: Put the GRUB commands in order to start a Linux system by hand.

items.t: `set root=(hd0,1)`
items.why: Choose the partition that holds the kernel.

items.t: `linux /boot/vmlinuz root=/dev/sda1`
items.why: Load the kernel and tell it where the root file system is.

items.t: `initrd /boot/initrd.img`
`boot`

questions.title: What the kernel does first
questions.text: After the boot loader hands over control, what does the kernel do before it starts the first process?

options.t: It detects CPU and memory, sets up memory and devices, mounts the root file system, then starts PID 1.
It starts all the daemons itself, one after the other, before any other process exists.
It asks the user which services to start, and waits for the answer at the console.
It formats the disks that it finds, so that the file systems are ready for the services that start afterwards.

questions.title: initrd
questions.text: What is the initial RAM disk (initrd / initramfs)?

options.t: A small temporary root file system in memory, with the tools needed to find the real root file system.
options.why: Discarded after the real root is mounted.

options.t: A backup of the home directory of the user, which the kernel restores at each boot.
The swap partition, which the kernel uses as extra memory while the system is starting and before RAM is ready.
A list of the services to start, which the kernel passes on to the first process.

questions.title: Root mounted read-only
questions.text: Why does the kernel often mount the root file system read-only at first?

options.t: So it can be checked (fsck) safely before anything writes to it; it is remounted read-write later.
Because the kernel cannot write to any disk until the first user has logged in.
Because the root disk is always a CD or a DVD, which can only be read.
Because the permissions of the root file system forbid even the root user to write in it during the whole boot.

questions.title: Low PIDs
questions.text: Match each process with its role.

pairs.r: The kernel's idle/scheduler task (not a normal process)
The first user-space process, `init`, today usually `systemd`

extras.r: The first process of the machine, `bash`
extras.why: Your shell comes much later, started by PID 1 through login.

questions.title: Kernel messages
questions.text: Which command shows the messages the kernel printed during boot (hardware detection, drivers)?

options.t: `dmesg`
options.why: It prints the kernel ring buffer.

options.t: `history`
`last`
`uname`
options.why: Shows the kernel name and version only.

questions.title: Kernel parameters
questions.text: What can you pass to the kernel from the boot loader?

options.t: Options such as the root device, `single` or `systemd.unit=rescue.target` (a repair mode).
options.why: They modify how the kernel and PID 1 start.

options.t: New passwords for the user accounts, which the kernel stores in the shadow file.
Shell aliases, which the first process loads before it starts the login shells.
The date and time of the next shutdown, which the kernel then schedules for the machine and announces to the users.

questions.title: The first process
questions.text: What is the role of the process with PID 1?

options.t: It starts and supervises the services, adopts orphaned processes and gives access to the system.
options.why: On modern Linux it is usually systemd.

options.t: It is the same thing as the kernel, only running in user mode and with a lower priority than the other processes.
It exists only while the machine shuts down, where it stops all the other processes.
It is the shell of the first user who logs in, and every other process is its child.
options.why: It starts before any user logs in.

questions.title: Kinds of init system
questions.text: Match each system with its family.

pairs.r: The classic sequential start with scripts in `/etc/init.d`
The modern parallel, dependency-based manager, standard on most distributions
The approach of FreeBSD, OpenBSD and NetBSD

extras.r: The init system of Linux, GRUB
extras.why: GRUB is the boot loader; it runs before the init system.

questions.title: Advantages of systemd
questions.text: Select the features that systemd offers.

options.t: Starts services in parallel, following declared dependencies.
Can restart services that crash.
Tracks the processes of a service with control groups (cgroups), not just PIDs.
options.why: Finds all children of a service.

options.t: Can start services on demand (for example when a socket or device appears).
Needs a graphical desktop to work.
Replaces the kernel.
options.why: It runs on top of it.

questions.title: What is a unit
questions.text: What is a systemd "unit"?

options.t: A configuration file describing something systemd manages: a service, a mount, a socket, a timer, a target...
options.why: Named with a suffix such as `.service` or `.target`.

options.t: A measure of CPU time, which systemd uses to share the processor between all the services that are running.
A single running process, started and watched by systemd until it stops.
options.why: A unit describes it; the process is separate.

options.t: A user account of the system, with its home directory and its login shell.

questions.title: Unit types
questions.text: Match each unit type with its purpose.

pairs.r: A daemon or program that systemd runs
A group of units that marks a state of the system

pairs.why: Generated from `/etc/fstab` or written by hand.

pairs.r: A schedule that triggers another unit
A network or local socket that can start a service on demand

extras.why: Accounts live in `/etc/passwd`; `.user` is not a unit type.

questions.title: Where units live
questions.text: Where are the unit files shipped by packages usually stored, and where do administrators put their own changes?

options.t: Packages install them in `/lib/systemd/system`; local units and overrides go in `/etc/systemd/system`, which wins.
options.why: Do not edit the package files.

options.t: Both in `/bin`, where the programs of the system are stored, and nowhere else.
Packages in `/etc/systemd/system` and the local files in `/tmp`, which is cleaned up at every boot of the machine.
Only in the home directory of the user who administers the machine, in a hidden folder.

questions.title: What a target is
questions.text: What is a target in systemd?

options.t: A named group of units that represents a stage or state of the system, replacing the older runlevels.
options.why: Reaching a target means its units are started.

options.t: A file that stores the partition table of the disk that the system starts from.
A way to direct the output of a program to the printer that is configured as the default printer of the system.
The kernel's target CPU, for which the machine code of the programs was compiled.

questions.title: Runlevels and targets
questions.text: Match each classic runlevel with its systemd target.

extras.why: That is a real target, but it has no classic runlevel number.

questions.title: Default target
questions.text: Which command shows the target that the system boots into?

options.t: `systemctl get-default`
options.why: Often `graphical.target` on desktops and `multi-user.target` on servers.

options.t: `systemctl status`
options.why: Shows the state of the system and services.

options.t: `runlevel 5`
`who -r`
options.why: Only reports the runlevel on some systems.

questions.title: Change target now
questions.text: What does `systemctl isolate rescue.target` do?

options.t: It stops the services that do not belong to the rescue target and brings the machine into maintenance mode.
options.why: It switches the running system to that target.

options.t: It makes rescue mode the default for all the boots that follow, but does not change the state of the running system.
It deletes the unit file of the target, so that it cannot be used again.
It isolates the network cable of the machine, by disabling the network interfaces.

questions.title: Set the default
questions.text: Make the system boot to text mode (without graphical login) next time: `systemctl {{0}} multi-user.target`
questions.note: `isolate` switches now; `set-default` decides the next boots.

wrong.why: That changes the running state now but not the next boot.
That enables a unit to start at boot; it does not choose the default target.

questions.title: Basic systemctl actions
questions.text: Match each command with its effect.

pairs.why: It runs until stopped or shutdown.
It stays enabled for the next boot if it was.

pairs.r: Show its state, recent log lines and whether it is enabled
Ask it to re-read its configuration without stopping
pairs.why: Only if the service supports it.

extras.why: None of these commands does that; `systemctl cups` without an action is not even valid.

questions.title: enable versus start
questions.text: What is the difference between `systemctl start ssh` and `systemctl enable ssh`?

options.t: `start` runs the service now; `enable` makes it start automatically at boot but does not start it now.
They are identical, and both start the service and make it start again at each boot.
`enable` starts the service only for the root user, while `start` does it for everyone who is logged in to the system.
`start` makes the service start at every boot, while `enable` runs it once only.
options.why: It affects the current session only.

questions.title: disable versus stop
questions.text: What does `systemctl disable ssh` do?

options.t: It removes the automatic start at boot but leaves the running service running.
options.why: Combine with `stop` to end it now.

options.t: It stops the service immediately.
It deletes the package.
It prevents the service from being started again, even manually, until you run `enable` once more.
options.why: That is what `mask` does; `disable` only removes the automatic start at boot.

questions.title: Mask
questions.text: What does `systemctl mask ssh` achieve beyond `disable`?

options.t: It links the unit to `/dev/null`, so it cannot be started at all: not at boot, manually or as a dependency.
It hides the service from `ps`, so that its processes no longer appear in the list.
It makes the log of the service quieter, by discarding all the messages that have a low priority in the journal.
It is the same as `restart`, with a different name that is used for unit files.

questions.title: Start and enable together
questions.text: Start the service now and also at every boot: `systemctl {{0}} ssh`
questions.note: Equivalent to `systemctl enable ssh` followed by `systemctl start ssh`.

wrong.why: It would run the service but not enable it for boot.

questions.title: Is it running
questions.text: Which command prints `active` or `inactive` for a service so a script can test it?

options.t: `systemctl is-active ssh`
options.why: Its exit status is 0 when the unit is active.

options.t: `systemctl list ssh`
`systemctl show`
`ps ssh`

questions.title: Old-style commands
questions.text: On many systems `service cups start` and `/etc/init.d/cups start` still exist. What are they?

options.t: The System V way of controlling a service; `service` forwards to `systemctl`, but running the script directly bypasses systemd.
The only possible ways to control a service, on any system that is in use today, whatever its init system may be.
Commands that delete the service and its unit file from the machine for good.
Commands that are available only to root, and refused for every ordinary user.
options.why: Regular users may need `sudo` for both.

questions.title: Service logs
questions.text: Which command shows the log messages of the service `ssh` collected by systemd?

options.t: `journalctl -u ssh`
options.why: Reads the journal and filters by unit.

options.t: `dmesg -u ssh`
`last ssh`
`systemctl log ssh`

questions.title: Failed units
questions.text: Which command lists the units that failed to start?

options.t: `systemctl --failed`
options.why: A quick health check after boot.

options.t: `systemctl list-failures`
`journalctl -f`
options.why: Follows new messages, not failed units.

options.t: `systemctl is-enabled`
options.why: Reports the enabled state of one unit.

questions.title: Dependencies
questions.text: What does it mean when a unit file says `After=network.target` and `Wants=network.target`?

options.t: The service starts after the network target is reached, and systemd tries to bring the network up as well.
options.why: `After` sets ordering; `Wants` sets a soft dependency.

options.t: The service starts before the network target is reached, in order to prepare the network for its own needs first.
The service is deleted whenever the network goes down, and installed again afterwards.
The service controls the network, and starts and stops it as it is needed.

questions.title: Restart on failure
questions.text: Which setting in a service unit makes systemd start the program again when it crashes?

options.t: `Restart=on-failure` (in the `[Service]` section)
`After=crash.target`, which orders the service after the crash
`Enabled=yes`, which keeps the service alive at every moment
`WantedBy=failure`, which links the service to the failure target

questions.title: Shutdown commands
questions.text: Match each command with its effect.

extras.r: Kill every user session and delete their files
extras.why: No option does that; `shutdown -k` only sends the warnings, without shutting down.

questions.title: Who can shut down
questions.text: Who may normally run `shutdown` on a multi-user system?

options.t: Only root (for example with `sudo`).
Any logged-in user.
Only the first user who logged in.
Only the user `nobody`.

questions.title: What happens at shutdown
questions.text: Put the stages of a clean shutdown in order.

items.t: Users are warned with a message
items.why: So they can save their work.

items.t: Processes receive `SIGTERM` and services are stopped in order
Processes that survive the grace period receive `SIGKILL`
File systems are synchronised and unmounted
items.why: Write buffers to disk, then detach.

items.t: The machine powers off or reboots

questions.title: Why SIGTERM first
questions.text: Why does the shutdown sequence send `SIGTERM` before `SIGKILL`?

options.t: Programs can catch `SIGTERM` to save data and exit cleanly; only those that do not finish in time get `SIGKILL`.
Because `SIGKILL` cannot be sent to services, only to the processes of ordinary users that have a terminal.
Because `SIGTERM` powers off the hardware, while `SIGKILL` only ends the processes.
Because `SIGKILL` is slower than `SIGTERM`, and the shutdown has to be done quickly.

questions.title: Why unmount
questions.text: Why must file systems be unmounted (or remounted read-only) before power off?

options.t: Data may still be waiting in memory buffers; unmounting writes it to disk and marks the file system clean.
options.why: A sudden power cut can leave inconsistencies.

options.t: Because unmounted disks use less electricity, which matters when a laptop is running on its battery.
Because the kernel would otherwise refuse to power off, until every disk has been unmounted.
To delete the temporary files that the programs have left on the disk before the machine stops.

questions.title: Custom shutdown message
questions.text: Which command warns users with your own message and shuts down in 10 minutes?

options.t: `shutdown -h +10 "Maintenance in 10 minutes"`
options.why: The text is sent to all terminals.

options.t: `shutdown -c "Maintenance"`, which announces the message and then goes on
`echo Maintenance | shutdown`, which reads the message from its input
options.why: The message is not read from stdin.

options.t: `halt +10`, which stops the machine after a delay of ten minutes

questions.title: Reboot shortcut
questions.text: What is a normal effect of pressing `Ctrl+Alt+Del` on a Linux text console?

options.t: It triggers a reboot through the init system (systemd maps it to `reboot.target`).
options.why: On many systems it can be disabled.

options.t: It opens a task manager where you can choose which processes to end, as in Windows.
It locks the screen and asks for the password of the user before anything else happens.
Nothing at all, because the kernel ignores that key combination on a text console.
options.why: The kernel passes the key combination to the init system.

questions.title: fstab
questions.text: What is `/etc/fstab` used for?

options.t: It lists the file systems (device, mount point, type, options) that are mounted at boot.
It stores the passwords of the users, in a form that only the administrator can read.
It holds the boot menu of GRUB, with one entry for each kernel that is installed.
It records who logged in and when, which `last` later reads to show the history.

questions.title: Swap
questions.text: What is swap space?

options.t: Disk space that the kernel can use to hold memory pages that are not in use, making more room in RAM.
A directory for temporary files, which programs fill while they run and the system then cleans.
A special user account that owns the files which the kernel moves between disks.
A backup of the `/home` directory, which is made automatically at every shutdown.

questions.title: Clean /tmp
questions.text: Why do many systems clean `/tmp` at boot?

options.t: Temporary files are not meant to survive a reboot, and leftovers could fill the disk or confuse programs.
Because `/tmp` is stored inside the boot loader, which clears it at every start.
Because the kernel cannot mount the file system of `/tmp` while that directory still holds files from the last session.
To remove the passwords that the users have typed into programs during the last session.

questions.title: Restart a service
questions.text: Stop and start the service `cron` again in one command: `systemctl {{0}} cron`

wrong.why: That asks the program to re-read its configuration without stopping it.
That only sets the automatic start at boot.

questions.title: Start at boot and now
questions.text: Start `nginx` now and also at every boot: `systemctl {{0}} nginx`

wrong.why: That starts it now, but it will not start at boot.
That sets the start at boot, but does not start it now.

questions.title: Power off in ten minutes
questions.text: Power the machine off in ten minutes: `shutdown {{0}}`
questions.note: `shutdown -c` cancels it before the time is up.

questions.text: Classify each step of the boot.

items.t: The firmware tests the hardware
GRUB shows the menu
The firmware reads the partition table
PID 1 starts the services
The root file system is remounted read-write
The login prompt appears

questions.text: Select the kinds of unit that systemd can manage.

options.t: A service such as `ssh.service`
A mount point such as `home.mount`
A timer such as `backup.timer`
A target such as `multi-user.target`
A user password
A regular text file in `/home`

questions.text: Put the commands in order to make a server boot without a graphical login from now on.

items.t: `systemctl get-default`
items.why: Look at the current default first.

items.t: `sudo systemctl set-default multi-user.target`
items.why: Change the default for the next boots.

items.t: `sudo reboot`
items.why: Restart so the change takes effect.

items.t: `systemctl get-default`

questions.text: Match each command with its effect.

pairs.r: Shuts down and powers off the machine

pairs.why: Only before the time is up.
